abstract.p: This document defines a file system API for XPath 4.0. It defines extension functions to perform file system related operations such as listing, reading, or writing files or directories.
The document is an update of the original specification, developed by the EXPath Community Group, defined for XPath 2.0 and published in 2015.
The update takes advantage of optional parameters and other features of XPath 4.0, adds new functions, and clarifies or revises the behavior of existing functions.
These functions are defined for use in , , , and other related XML standards.
A summary of changes since published version 1.0 is provided at .

status.p: This version of the specification is work in progress. It is produced by the QT4 Working Group, officially the W3C XSLT 4.0 Extensions Community Group. Individual functions specified in the document may be at different stages of review, reflected in their History notes. Comments are invited, in the form of GitHub issues at https://github.com/qt4cg/qtspecs.

note.p: The publications of this community group are dedicated to our co-chair, Michael Sperberg-McQueen (1954–2024).

div1.head: Introduction

changes.change: If a section of this specification has been updated since version 1.0, an overview of the changes is provided, along with links to navigate to the next or previous change.
Sections with significant changes are marked with a ✭ symbol in the table of contents. New functions are indicated by ✚.

div1.p: The purpose of this document is to define functions to access and manipulate files and directories of a local file system, for inclusion in XPath 4.0, XQuery 4.0, and XSLT 4.0.
The exact syntax used to call these functions is specified in , , and .
This document defines several classes of functions:

item.p: Functions to examine the properties of files, such as size and modification dates.
Functions to perform basic operations on files as entities, such as copying, moving, deleting, and creating directories and temporary files.
Functions to read from and write to files in various formats.
Functions to access and manipulate file paths.

Functions to examine properties of the underlying file system and current context, such as establishing the current working directory or the characters used for various separators within paths or files.

div1.p: References to specific sections of other specifications are indicated by cross-document links in this document. Each such link consists of a pointer to a specific section followed by a superscript specifying the linked document. The superscripts have the following meanings: BIN40 , FO , and XP .

div2.head: Error management
div2.p: Error conditions are identified by a code (a QName). When such an error condition is reached in the evaluation of an expression, a is raised with the corresponding error code, as if the function fn:error had been called.

In this specification these codes use the http://expath.org/ns/file namespace and a “descriptive string” local part, e.g. , rather than the http://www.w3.org/2005/xqt-errors namespace and alphanumeric local part, e.g. err:FOCH0004, used in .

div2.head: File paths
div2.p: File paths are specified as strings.

The current working directory is an absolute implementation-defined directory against which all relative file paths are resolved. For example, it can be the directory from which a query processor was started.

If the points to a local directory, the base directory is this directory; if it points to a local file, it is the directory of this file. Otherwise, it is undefined. file:base-dir can be used to retrieve the directory. A file path can be resolved against this directory by simply appending it (if it is relative), or by calling file:resolve-path:
An implementation must accept absolute and relative UNIX-based and Windows paths as well as absolute file URIs. Some examples:

item.p: C:\Test Dir\my file.xml: an absolute path on Windows platforms.
/Test Dir/my file.xml: an absolute path on UNIX-based platforms.
C:\\\Test Dir//\\my file.xml: an absolute path on Windows platforms with redundant slashes and backslashes.
my file.xml: a relative path, pointing to a file in the current working directory.
file:///C:/Test%20Dir/my%20file.xml: an absolute file URI on Windows platforms.
file:///Test%20Dir/my%20file.xml: an absolute file URI on UNIX-based platforms.

div2.p: A file URI is converted to a path as described for the filepath entry of fn:parse-uri.

Before further processing, all paths are normalized to an implementation-dependent representation (which usually is the representation of the underlying operating system), with operating-system-specific directory separators.

It is implementation-dependent whether the error is raised by any function of this module that accepts a path argument if a path is invalid, i.e., if it contains characters that are not allowed in a specific file system. For this reason, the error is not listed with the individual functions.
Whenever a function generates a path that is known to refer to a directory, it will be suffixed with the operating-system-specific directory separator.
Whenever a function generates a path by appending a name or a relative path to a supplied directory path, a directory separator is inserted only if the supplied path does not already end with one.

Some operating systems may use paths to identify objects other than files, directories, or symbolic links: for example, hardware devices. The effect of using such paths with the functions in this library is implementation-defined.

div2.head: Symbolic links
div2.p: A symbolic link is a file that contains a reference to another file or directory, as defined in .
The functions of this module treat a symbolic link as the file or directory that it refers to, with the following exceptions:

item.p: file:delete removes the symbolic link itself; the file or directory that it refers to is left untouched.
It is implementation-defined whether file:copy and file:move operate on the symbolic link or on the file or directory that it refers to.
It is implementation-defined whether the functions that traverse a directory recursively descend into symbolic links that refer to a directory.

div2.head: Function execution
div2.p: Many functions in this library are marked as nondeterministic, which means they are not guaranteed to perform the same operations and produce identical results when being called repeatedly.
For example, the expression:
div2.eg: ( file:append-text($file, "first line"), file:append-text($file, "second line"), file:append-text($file, "third line") )
div2.p: will produce the expected outcome only if the three subexpressions are fully evaluated, in order. This requires the optimizer to exercise restraint, as described in .

A processor that supports the functions in this library must therefore ensure that these functions are not relocated or pre-evaluated and that their results are not cached when compiling and evaluating the query and serializing its results.

Equally, users need to ensure that calls to such functions are statically explicit and that they occur only in contexts where the order of execution is predictable. Dynamic calls on these functions are likely to have unpredictable effects, as are calls appearing in contexts where strict order of evaluation cannot be assumed (for example, when computing sort keys).

div2.head: Conformance
div2.p: This specification follows the general remarks on and terminology for conformance given in .
In this document, text labeled as an example or as a note is provided for explanatory purposes and is not normative.

div2.head: Namespaces and prefixes
div2.p: The functions defined in this document are contained exclusively in the namespace http://expath.org/ns/file and referenced using an xs:QName binding to that namespace.

This document uses the prefix file to refer to this namespace. User-written applications can choose a different prefix to refer to the namespace, so long as it is bound to the correct URI. In accordance with current practice, it is recommended that the prefix file be reserved for use with this namespace.

div2.head: Function signatures and descriptions
div2.p: Each function (or group of functions having the same name) is defined in this specification using a standard proforma, full details of which can be found in . In this version, optional parameters (introduced in XPath 4.0) are used where appropriate, rather than multiple signatures with different arities.

note.p: If no argument is supplied for a parameter that has a default value, the default value is used. If the parameter is marked (:default-on-empty:), the default value is also used when the supplied argument is the empty sequence. Otherwise, the empty sequence is treated according to the function-specific rules.
The marker is only used on parameters that have default values.

div1.head: Error summary
div1.p: The error text provided with these errors is non-normative.

error.p: The target path of a copy or move operation is located inside the source directory.
The specified path does not exist.
The specified path does not point to a directory.
The specified path points to a directory.
The specified encoding is not supported.
The specified offset or length is negative, or the chosen values would exceed the file bounds.
A generic file system error occurred.

item.p: The function signatures now use the optional parameter syntax of XPath 4.0 where appropriate, rather than giving several signatures of differing arity. Changes to the semantics of individual functions are listed in .

inform-div1.head: Compatibility with Previous Versions
inform-div1.p: This section summarizes the extent to which this specification is compatible with previous versions.
Due to optional parameters, calls such as file:list($dir, false(), ()), which were invalid in 1.0 because $pattern had the type xs:string, are now valid and select the default behavior.
Version 4.0 of this function library is fully backwards compatible with version 1.0, except as noted below:

item.p: file:delete no longer raises an error if the specified path does not exist.
file:copy and file:move raise if the target path is located inside the source directory.

If no encoding is supplied, file:read-text and file:read-text-lines recognize a UTF-16 byte order mark, and they raise an error for characters that cannot be decoded unless the fallback option is enabled.
file:resolve-path normalizes absolute paths as well, and it preserves a trailing directory separator.
If the points to a directory, file:base-dir returns this directory instead of its parent directory.
